entities.name: Alexander Neville
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander Neville (c. 1340–1392) was Archbishop of York from 1374 until his translation and fall in 1388, a leading northern English churchman whose career was entangled with the politics of Edward III’s last years and the reign of Richard II. A member of the powerful Neville family, he rose through royal and papal favour to the second see of England, administering a vast northern province and sitting among the realm’s great prelates. His archiepiscopate coincided with fiscal strain, court faction, and the rising assertiveness of the Commons.

In 1388 the Merciless Parliament and the Lords Appellant moved against Richard II’s favourites; Neville was impeached, deprived of York, and translated against his will to the titular see of St Andrews—effectively exile from English power—before fleeing abroad. He died in Louvain in 1392. Neville’s fall illustrates how late medieval English archbishops could be broken by aristocratic faction even when backed by kinship networks, and how York’s political weight made its incumbent a prize and a target in Ricardian politics.
